name: US state PFAS product restriction effective dates by category
description: State-by-state PFAS product ban and restriction effective dates. Each record is one state’s ban on one product category, with the effective date, the statute or bill number, the enforcement agency, and any exemptions (e.g. currently unavoidable use). Answers 'can I sell [product] containing PFAS in [state] after [date]', 'which states ban PFAS in cookware', 'when does [state] ban all PFAS products'. Roughly 30 jurisdictions with active or pending PFAS product restrictions as of mid-2026, each with different product category definitions and phase-in schedules.

Maryland Maryland’s HB 1147 (effective January 1, 2024) banned PFAS in food packaging, rugs, carpets, and firefighting foam.

New Hampshire Governor Kelly Ayotte (R) signed <https://gc.nh.gov/bill_status/billinfo.aspx?PastId=147&sy=2025&id=99999> NH HB 167 , prohibiting the sale of ski, boat, and board waxes containing intentionally added PFAS.
Effective January 1, 2026: Cleaning products Cookware Dental floss Menstruation products Ski wax Textile articles Outdoor apparel for severe wet conditions

products with intentionally added PFAS in these categories can still be sold, but only if the manufacturer labels them and notifies Connecticut DEEP: Apparel Carpets and rugs Cleaning products Cookware Cosmetics Dental floss Fabric treatments Juvenile products Menstrual products Textile furnishings Ski wax Upholstered furniture January 1, 2028 (full ban): intentionally added PFAS is prohibited outright in all of the categories above, plus outdoor apparel for severe wet conditions. Outdoor apparel for severe wet conditions also carries an earlier “Made with PFAS chemicals” disclosure requirement starting January 1, 2026.

records.source_quote: California has multiple overlapping PFAS laws. AB 1817 bans textile articles (clothing, bedding, towels) with intentionally added PFAS. Effective January 1, 2025 , with outdoor apparel for severe wet conditions following on January 1, 2028.

Colorado Colorado’s HB22-1345, expanded by SB24-081 in 2024, established a phased ban on intentionally added PFAS. Effective January 1, 2024: Carpets and rugs Fabric treatments Food packaging Juvenile products Oil and gas products Cosmetics Indoor and outdoor textile furnishings Indoor and outdoor upholstered furniture Effective January 1, 2025: Disclosure requirement for outdoor apparel used in severe wet conditions Effective January 1, 2026: Cleaning products Cookware Dental floss Menstruation products Ski wax Textile articles
